source.title: Derailing Non-Answers via Logit Suppression at Output Subspace Boundaries in RLHF-Aligned Language Models
source.authors: Harvey Dam; Jonas Knochelmann; Vinu Joseph; Ganesh Gopalakrishnan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports refusal-related outcomes from suppressing output tokens, but does not measure, remove, add, or test the difference-in-means refusal direction or any other versioned claim. It cites the original study and contrasts its method with abliteration.
record.gate_note: The paper reports changes in answer/refusal outcomes after suppressing newline and EOS logits. Those findings concern a token-level generation intervention, not the direction or mechanisms specified by V1–V8; the reported outcomes are recorded as findings that fit no version. The paper also makes a general claim about standard benchmarks without giving benchmark names or results in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study suppresses the logits of two output tokens (\n\n after <think>, and optionally EOS after </think>) at generation time in DeepSeek-R1 distillations. It never computes, ablates, adds or edits a difference-in-means activation direction, and never measures one inside any model. Its 'refusal subspace' is an output-trajectory notion, not a residual-stream direction. The models do reason before answering, but no result bears on whether V1 holds in them (V8). The attack works without touching any direction, and nothing tests whether it suppresses one (V3). The only reference to abliteration is an unsupported assertion that it is 'more effective' and can improve benchmarks. That assertion comes with no experiment. The original is cited (misattributed to Azaria & Mitchell) and contrasted, so the relation is discusses / T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the authors' central interpretation: in the models tested, censorship appears implemented through localized generation patterns rather than knowledge removal. On this reading, 'unlearned' knowledge stays accessible through targeted decoding steering. The authors concede abliteration is much more effective but needs parameters and knowledge of the censored content.
record.recipe_differences: The study suppresses output-token logits at generation-time positions; it does not find a harmful-minus-harmless activation direction or ablate/add that direction. The paper says abliteration requires model parameters and knowledge of censored content and is more effective at removing censored answers.
record.method_sensitivity: The intervention is position-specific: newline suppression follows <think>, and optional EOS suppression follows </think>. The paper reports that EOS suppression's effect is not uniform across dataset-model pairs. Experiments use temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, and repetition penalty 1.1.

fits_no_version.finding: In four DeepSeek-R1 distillations, suppressing \n\n right after <think> significantly raised 'answered' rates on political-censorship prompts (CCP, DECCP). Adding EOS suppression after </think> helped in most pairs but was non-uniform: it sometimes raised refusal or evasive propaganda, and it raised empty final responses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Censorship-style refusals in R1 distillations are gated by an output-token branching point (<think>\n\n) that can be blocked at decoding time without any activation-space intervention.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code will be uploaded to a public repository or supplementary material if possible.
record.problems: The exact response proportions are presented in figures without numerical values in the supplied text. The text does not identify which particular dataset-model pairs account for the reported nonuniform EOS effects. The paper says it did not analyze internal activations. Its general statement about standard benchmark performance is not accompanied here by benchmark names or results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. CoT coherence/relevance outcomes were not extracted because they are not measures of the refusal behavior or direction specified by the claim.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed, ablated or added; capability retention under ablation is not measured.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed. The claim that abliteration is more effective is asserted without data.
The token-suppression attack is not linked to any activation direction, and there is no adversarial training against ablation.
Harm judgment and refusal are not separated.
DECCP mixes English and Chinese prompts, but no direction transfer across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
The reasoning models are tested only with output-token suppression; the direction is not examined in them. The authors state they did not analyze internal activations.

missing.what: The claimed 'no degradation on standard benchmarks' has no benchmark names or numbers in the text. It cannot serve as a capability check, and the record's capability_check 'y' should be 'n' or 'claimed only'.

record.verdict_notes: The refused content here is Chinese political censorship, not harmful-request refusal, so even the construct differs from the original's harmful-vs-harmless setup. The paper attributes arXiv:2406.11717 to 'Azaria & Mitchell' (actually Arditi et al.). The per-model p-value alignment in Figures 5 and 6 is reconstructed from scrambled figure text, and exact proportions are figure-only. The record's capability_check should not be 'y'.

versions.untested_parts: Does not identify or intervene on a difference-in-means direction, test its causal role, induce refusals by adding it, or measure preserved capabilities under its ablation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is performed.
The attack suppresses output-token logits, not the claimed residual-stream direction; it does not test training against that direction's ablation.
No comparison of single-direction, affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
The prompts include English and Chinese, but the paper does not test transfer of the direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No comparison of refusal training methods, stages, or resulting direction structure.
The models use chain-of-thought tokens, but the paper does not test the claimed direction in reasoning models.

rows.subject: DeepSeek-R1 distillation (Qwen 7B)
rows.operation_detail: Suppress the newline token immediately after <think> during generation.
rows.measure: Proportion of final responses classified as answered
rows.uncertainty: Fisher's exact test, baseline vs newline suppression: p=6.85e-11
rows.note: The paper says newline suppression greatly increased answered responses overall, but the exact plotted proportion for this model and dataset is not stated in the text.

rows.subject: DeepSeek-R1 distillation (Qwen 7B)
rows.operation_detail: Suppress the newline token after <think> and suppress EOS after </think> during generation.
rows.measure: Proportion of final responses classified as answered
rows.uncertainty: Fisher's exact test, baseline vs newline-and-EOS suppression: p=2.12e-11
rows.note: The paper says EOS suppression succeeded in most dataset-model pairs, but does not identify the result for this pair in the text.
